title: Kongo Gumi: A Family Firm for Fourteen Centuries
text:
In 578, according to the company's records, Prince Shotoku of Japan brought skilled carpenters from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build Shitenno-ji, a great Buddhist temple in what is now Osaka. One of them, Shigemitsu Kongo, stayed on. His family founded Kongo Gumi, a construction company that went on to build and repair temples for more than fourteen hundred years, longer than any other known company.

The family kept the business alive through wars, fires and the rise and fall of dynasties. One of its customs was that the leadership did not automatically pass to the eldest son. The family chose the most capable heir, and when no son was suitable, a talented son-in-law could be adopted into the family and take the Kongo name. In the 1930s, when the 37th leader died, his widow Yoshie Kongo took charge, the first woman to lead the firm. During the Second World War, when no one was building temples, the company survived by making wooden coffins.

In the 1980s Kongo Gumi borrowed heavily to invest in property during Japan's bubble economy. When land prices collapsed, the debts became too much. In 2006, after some forty generations of family ownership, its assets were taken over by the Takamatsu Construction Group, which kept it running as a subsidiary. The family scrolls tracing its lineage survive.
lesson: A family enterprise lasts by choosing successors for ability, not birth order. Even fourteen centuries of care can be undone by one generation's reckless borrowing.
people: Shigemitsu Kongo, the Kongo family, Yoshie Kongo
source: Kongo Gumi company records; reporting on the 2006 takeover (Bloomberg Businessweek, 2007)
caveat: The founding date and early history come from the company's own traditional records.
